method: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. A writer keeps two stocks of familiar words. Stock A is the word list of the public training pages carrying Currier's label A, stock B the list of those carrying B, and a third, smaller list serves the pages Currier left unlabelled; each stock also carries an order-3 glyph chain over its own words, used only for words the stock has never had. The writer works through the book in order and, on each page, takes up the stock of that page: it reaches for a word of the stock, drawn from the stock's own frequency list; with probability 0.10 it instead writes a word the stock has never had, shaped by that stock's glyph chain; with probability 0.15 it alters one glyph of whatever it just chose; and with probability 0.25, before any of that, it re-writes a word it has already written at least twice among the last 300 words. It keeps the manuscript's line lengths and writes paragraph-opening lines like any other line. No rule names a shared word, one page being alike to another, or the statistic: the sharing between pages of one stock is what sampling from a finite list does by itself. DISCLOSURE, because it decides what this is worth: the procedure switches stock on the page's Currier label, public metadata pinned in the repo for all 226 pages (Currier 1976), in the same way the generators on this record switch on the paragraph mark or the section. It is therefore the two-tables-per-dialect writer P-G-018 describes, and what is new here is not the two stocks but the rotation null: P-G-018's version passed the deal null on 2 of 3 seeds and the rotation null on none of 3. Control that fixes what carries it: the same writer with ONE stock for the whole book, labels ignored, everything else alike, gives -0.055, -0.061, -0.053 on seeds 1 to 3 and fails. Nothing was tuned against the fact: a hot-core boost was tried at 2 to 30 times, found unnecessary and dropped, so the submitted text uses each stock's plain frequencies; the reuse and variation settings (0.25 from 300 words, glyph change 0.15, fresh word 0.10, order-3 chain) were taken from the published line chain of R-017 and left alone. Local check on the practice split, where the fact stands at 0.122 with shuffle p = 0.005 and rotation p = 0.0294 at its floor of 1/34: this text (seed 1) gives 0.139, shuffle p = 0.005, rotation p = 0.0294, and its observed value exceeds the LARGEST of the 33 label rotations (0.054) by +0.085. Five further seeds give 0.066, 0.087, 0.114, 0.117, 0.122, all passing both nulls, with rotation margins +0.056 and +0.082 on the two further seeds measured. The margin is real where the manuscript's is not: F-020's own note says the rotation null has no margin at this sample size, and this text clears every shift on all six runs. Guards: 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 9,376 distinct words, mean length 4.9; the words are the manuscript's own, as a period word-list would use them, shared type share 0.85. What it shows, if it holds on the hidden pages: F-020 does not separate the dialect contrast from a writer who keeps two word-lists and takes them up in the book's order, including the long-range part the label rotation is meant to catch; the fact adds nothing to what the labels already say, and it is no evidence of meaning. What it does not show: that the manuscript was made that way. Assumption that could fail on the hidden pages: the hidden sample's own label layout decides the rotation null, and the margins above were measured on the practice sample of 29 labelled pages; a hidden sample made of longer unbroken runs of one label would leave a shift less to break.
